description: Moss green blotched with bark brown, dark veins branching in to one red knot at the middle. Filed with the blood stones.
lore: The trade sorts its stones by what they do rather than by what they came out of, and this one goes in the tray with the blood-natured: the ones that open a thing and hand some of it back to the arm that opened it. Whoever puts it there says the same sentence while doing it, which is that the only thing that ever ran in a Stumpling was sap. The word is wrong about the origin and exactly right about the behaviour, and there is no better word, so it stays and the caveat gets said aloud every time. It is the one stone on the bench that comes with an apology attached.

In the hand it is warm the way they are all warm, but not evenly. Roll it in the palm and there is a hot spot over the middle, and you can find it in a bag by feel alone. The green is not moss and not a coating; take a knife to it and you take off stone. Bark-brown blotches sit over the shoulder of it, the dark branching runs out from a knot low of centre and has gone brown well before it reaches the rim, and the red does not come to the surface anywhere. Handlers grade them on exactly that. A short bright knot with the veining still dark close in is what is wanted. The ones where the red has spread thin along the branches are weak in a blade, and everybody who has fitted both can tell you which they had.

What it does is take and give back. Set against an edge it lands heavier than a stone that size accounts for, and some of what it opens closes again on your side. That follows, once you think about who did the remembering. Hardly anyone remembers a forest on its own account; they remember having a use for one. Sap on the hands, the smell of a fresh cut, a load carried out at dusk and a winter that was warmer for it. Something is opened and the one who opened it goes home better off than they came, and that transaction is at the bottom of this creature, so that is what the stone does when it is set in a blade. There is no cruelty in it. It is being a wood, precisely as a wood was remembered.

It also settles a thing the creature will not. Everyone who has met one comes away with the same idea about that flat top, which is that something was done to it, and recently enough to be worth being careful about. The stone says otherwise. The cut is at the very bottom of the thing, harder and older than any part of it, and what is at the bottom is what a creature was assembled out of and never what happened to it later. It was not felled. It arrived felled. That is the sort of fact a stone will give you and the creature cannot: you could follow one through the trees for a season and learn none of it, since there is no mouth on it to say so and nothing red showing anywhere on the outside.
